planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings or divisions directly into saturated soil or an inch or two of standing water along a shaded stream edge, bog garden, or pond margin in spring; brooklime roots quickly from stem nodes and spreads on its own once established.

directions: Brooklime is a sprawling, hollow-stemmed European relative of watercress that naturally colonizes shaded spring heads, ditches, and slow streams, and it has long been gathered as a peppery salad and pot herb wherever it grows wild. Harvest the glossy, rounded leaf pairs and tender stem tips through the growing season for a crisp bite similar to watercress, used raw in salads or wilted briefly into soups. It needs constantly saturated or shallowly flooded soil to thrive and will wilt quickly if allowed to dry out, so it suits a bog bed or pond edge rather than an ordinary border. Established clumps root along their creeping stems and are easily divided and replanted through the season.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions into moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade after the last frost once soil has warmed; this understory ginger relative grows into a tall, leafy clump over its first full season and resents cold, wet soil while establishing.

directions: Malacca ginger is a tall Southeast Asian understory relative of galangal whose aromatic rhizome and young shoots are used in Malay and Indonesian cooking, adding a sharper, more floral note than common ginger to curries and sambals. In the garden it forms an upright clump of broad, glossy leaves on cane-like stems well suited to the dappled light beneath taller trees or shade structures in a warm, humid climate. Keep the soil consistently moist and rich in organic matter, since the shallow rhizome mat dries out and stalls growth quickly in sandy or compacted ground. Harvest rhizome pieces from the clump margin once plants are well established, leaving the center undisturbed to keep producing new shoots.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil in a shaded or semi-shaded, humid spot after frost danger has passed; clumps spread steadily and tolerate boggy ground better than most gingers.

directions: Tara is a vigorous ginger-family perennial of Northeast Indian and Southeast Asian forest understories, grown less for its fibrous rhizome than for its tender young shoots and inflorescences, which are boiled or stir-fried as a vegetable in Assamese and other regional cuisines. It forms large, cane-like clumps of broad leaves that handle wet, shaded ground far better than culinary ginger, making it useful at the damp, shady margin of a tropical kitchen garden. Cut young emerging shoots near the base while they are still pale and tender, before the fibrous outer leaves toughen. Divide crowded clumps every couple of years to renew vigor and control spread, since established plantings can form dense colonies in favorable conditions.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Sow seed in fall in a lightly shaded, well-drained bed so winter cold and moisture can break dormancy; this Siberian spring ephemeral emerges early and dies back to its underground corm by early summer, so mark the planting spot to avoid disturbing it while dormant.

directions: Siberian tuberous spring beauty is a small woodland ephemeral related to miner's lettuce, long gathered by indigenous peoples of Siberia and the Russian Far East for its starchy, chestnut-flavored corm, much as the related Claytonia lanceolata was used as an "Indian potato" in western North America. It pushes up a short rosette of fleshy leaves and pale pink flowers very early in spring beneath deciduous trees, then dies back underground by early summer once the tree canopy closes in. Corms are traditionally dug after a few seasons of undisturbed growth once they have bulked up, and can be boiled or roasted like a small potato. Grow it in a humus-rich woodland bed where it can be left undisturbed for several years between harvests, since digging too early yields little.
sources: Flora of China / Flora of Russia references

planting.note: Scatter seed or set small divisions onto the surface of moist soil in a shaded bed or container after the last frost; creeping wood sorrel germinates readily in warm weather and self-sows freely once a patch is established.

directions: Creeping wood sorrel is a low, mat-forming herb with clover-like leaflets and a bright, lemony-sour tang from the oxalic acid in its leaves and stems, used sparingly as a garnish, in salads, or as a tart flavoring much like sorrel. It spreads readily by rooting stems and explosive seed capsules in shaded containers, pathways, and bed margins, so it is best grown where some spread is welcome or kept in a pot to limit spontaneous spread. Because of its oxalic acid content it is traditionally eaten in small quantities rather than as a bulk salad green, and people prone to kidney stones are usually advised to limit intake. Snip leaves and stems continuously through the warm season for the best flavor, before older growth turns tougher and more acidic.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow onto consistently moist, shaded soil along a seep, streambank bed, or bog garden as soon as it can be worked in spring; this western North American native spreads by creeping stolons once it takes hold in reliably damp ground.

directions: Water chickweed is a small, succulent-leaved relative of miner's lettuce native to wet, shaded seeps and streambanks across western North America, where it was gathered by indigenous foragers as a mild, slightly succulent salad green. Its rounded leaves and creeping, rooting stems form a loose mat that spreads across saturated soil, making it a good choice for the damp margin of a shaded bog bed or rain garden rather than an ordinary dry border. Harvest the tender young leaves and stem tips continuously through the cool season, when the flavor is mildest and least bitter. Keep the planting site constantly wet, since the shallow roots and thin leaves wilt quickly if the soil is allowed to dry even briefly.
sources: Native American Ethnobotany Database (University of Michigan)
